manader.sub: Rest, ice and the slow return of the light
natur: In the middle of winter it can look as though nature has stopped. But whoever walks slowly along the pond on a clear January morning sees that it is full of life – only at another pace. Under the ice the frogs lie dormant in the mud on the bottom, and the dragonfly larvae move slowly in the cold water. In the compost, where the warmth of decomposition lingers, insects sleep and perhaps a hedgehog in the leaf pile beside it. Everything that needs to rest rests. Everything that needs to eat searches.

The birds are the most visible. Great tits, blue tits, marsh tits and nuthatches take turns at the bird table in the apple tree. The bullfinches come in small flocks and pick at buds and seeds, the males with their rose-red breasts against the snow. Some winters the waxwings appear, sometimes in their hundreds, and strip the rowans of berries in a few days before moving on. Over Ekoln the white-tailed eagle soars; in winter it often keeps to where the ice is open. And at dusk the tawny owl is heard from the nest box in the old oak.

Towards the end of the month something happens that many are waiting for. On a clear morning the great tit begins to sing its simple two-note song – tee-cha, tee-cha – from the top of a birch. It is not a spring song yet, but it is the promise of one. The ravens have already begun courting with acrobatic flights over the woods, and they are among the first to build a nest. The fox mates in January and February, and whoever lies awake one night may hear its hoarse bark from the edge of the woods.

The snow tells what has happened in the night. The fox’s track runs like a string of beads, each paw set in the last. The hare’s tracks come in pairs, the long hind feet in front of the short forefeet. Roe deer have walked along the hedge and browsed buds. Sometimes a track ends abruptly, with wing marks on either side – an owl or a hawk that has taken a vole. Every morning of fresh snow is a new page to read.
karaktar: January is the quietest month at Vreta. The pond lies under ice, the meadow under snow and the forest garden’s trees stand bare with buds that have not yet made up their minds. The café by the gate is closed, the tipi is packed away in the store and most guests have gone home after the holidays. What can be heard is the wind in the pines, snow slipping from a branch, the raven croaking over Ekoln and the fire crackling in the cottage stove.

But silence is not the same as standing still. Under the snow the soil lives on, slowly. In the orangery the lemon trees flower in the weak light and fill the room with a scent that seems almost improbable in midwinter. In the workshops winter’s work goes on: tools are sharpened, broken chairs glued and new frame drums stretched. On the kitchen table the seed packets lie spread out, and the site journal is open at last year’s pages. January is the month when the next year is planned – and when the last one is allowed to sink in.

The light comes back, but at its own pace. On 1 January the sun rises at 08.47 and sets as early as 14.58. A month later the day has grown by almost two hours. It shows first in the afternoons, when it is suddenly still light at four, and then in the mornings, when the snow glows blue before the sun has cleared the treetops.

We call the month’s full moon the Ice Moon. It rises on Friday 22 January, and it is the closest full moon of the year – only 357,600 kilometres away. Such a moon is sometimes called a supermoon. The difference is hard to see with the naked eye, but a clear, cold night with snow on the ground still makes it something special. It is light enough to walk to the sauna without a lantern.
himmel: January has the longest nights of the year after December, and they are often clear and cold. That makes it one of the best months for anyone who wants to see stars. Orion stands high in the south in the evenings, with Betelgeuse like a red lantern at his shoulder and Rigel a blue-white one at his foot. The Pleiades, the Seven Sisters, glimmer above. Lower in the east Leo rises and, at the end of the month, both Jupiter and Mars – two planets that reach their closest point in February.

The month begins with a gift: the Quadrantids, a meteor shower that peaks on the night between 3 and 4 January. The moon is then almost new and does not interfere. Whoever dresses warmly, lays a reindeer skin on a sun lounger and looks north-east after midnight can see many shooting stars. On the same mornings Venus shines as a brilliant morning star in the south-east. It is then furthest from the sun, and for the rest of the winter it sinks slowly towards the horizon.
citat: Nothing in nature is in a hurry in January. That is a lesson in itself.
manader.ingress: The year does not begin with a start. It begins with a rest – and with the light that stays a few minutes longer each day.

water: Ekoln

Dalkarlskärret and Stora kärret are frozen and silent. The reeds stand yellow, and in the snow on the ice are tracks of fox and roe deer that cross the fen rather than go round it.
The tarn

manader.sub: Beeswax candles, seed sowing and the first birdsong
natur: The sun has regained its strength. On a clear day at the end of February it can be several degrees below zero in the shade and still drip from the eaves on the south side of the cottage. The snow around the tree trunks melts first, since the dark bark takes up the warmth and radiates it, and the apple trees in the forest garden soon stand each in its own small hollow. When the sun softens the snow surface by day and the night freezes it to a crust, the snow crust forms. On an early morning it bears your weight, and then you can walk straight across the meadow without sinking through. By lunchtime it has often softened again.

The birds have begun counting the days. The great tit’s two-note song is heard every sunny morning, and great tits and blue tits start looking into the nest boxes and sitting in the entrance holes, as if trying them out for spring. The nuthatch whistles from the oak. The great spotted woodpecker drums on a dry branch so that it echoes across the pond – the drumming is the woodpecker’s song, a way of claiming territory and calling a mate. The wren, one of our smallest birds, sings with a surprisingly strong voice from the brush pile by the compost. And the ravens, which have been courting since January, are now building a nest, ideally high in an old pine. The female often lays her eggs as early as March, while the snow is still lying.

The nights belong to the owls and the foxes. The tawny owl often calls most in February and March, when the pairs decide where to nest – at best in the box in the old oak. The foxes’ mating season is drawing to an end, and the cubs are born in the earth in April or May. The badger does not sleep all winter but rests, and on a mild night it may come out and leave its broad, five-toed tracks in the snow. Badger cubs are born now, in February and March, deep in the sett.

Under the snow the plants are ready to go. In warm spots – by the cottage’s sill, against the stone wall and under the eaves of the orangery – the snowdrops may push up by the end of the month. The hazel catkins, which have sat short and hard on the branches since autumn, grow longer and yellower, and in a mild week they may begin to release their pollen. By the entrance it is often the corkscrew hazel that shows it first, its twisted branches full of yellow catkins. On a mild day the snow can also fill with small black dots that jump. They are springtails, called snow fleas, and they creep up out of the leaf litter when it thaws. They are harmless and a sign of how much life there is in the soil even now.
karaktar: February is the second half of winter, and it has a different tone from the first. The snow often lies deepest now, the cold can bite harder than in January and the pond still sleeps under the ice. But the light has changed character. It falls warmer through the orangery’s tall windows, it glitters on the snow crust in the meadow and it lingers in the birch tops when the path to the cottage has already turned blue. Whoever has walked to the hen house in the dark all winter notices one morning that they can see where they are putting their feet – and one afternoon that the lights in the workshop need not be switched on until after four.

The place still keeps winter’s pace. But the work has begun to turn outwards again. Under the grow lights in the greenhouse and in the cottage windows stand the first seed trays with chillies and sweet peppers, which need a long time to fruit in a Nordic summer. In the joinery nest boxes are built from old boards. In the workshop the wax from last summer’s honey harvest is melted, and newly dipped candles hang drying in long rows ahead of Candlemas.

February is also the month for seeing what is left. In the root cellar the crates of carrots, beetroot and apples have shrunk, and the woodpiles by the sauna have sunk. The old farmers’ almanac reckoned that half the winter was gone by Candlemas and that half the fodder should then remain. It is still a good rule. Whoever has more than half left can share. Whoever has less must eke it out until spring.

We call the month’s full moon the Light Moon, after the days, which now grow by a good five minutes a day. It is full at 00.23 in the night between Saturday 20 and Sunday 21 February, and the same night it slips through the earth’s penumbra in a faint eclipse. Mars, which was at opposition the day before, shines red a few degrees above. It is a night to be outside, however cold it gets.
himmel: February 2027 is the month of the planets. On 11 February Jupiter is at opposition, directly opposite the sun as seen from the earth. It rises in the east as the sun sets, stands highest in the south around midnight and sets in the west at dawn. It shines with a strong, steady yellow-white light in Leo, and in binoculars held steady against a door post its four largest moons can be seen as small points of light in a row. From evening to evening they change places.

Eight days later, on 19 February, it is Mars’s turn. Around 20 February the red planet shines only a few degrees from Regulus, the brightest star in Leo, and the difference in colour between them is easy to see. On the night between 19 and 20 February Mars is 101 million kilometres away, closer than at any time in the year. It is a fairly distant opposition – Mars’s orbit is oval, and at the closest oppositions the distance can fall below 60 million kilometres – but the planet still shines clearly all night.
citat: The light comes before the warmth. February teaches us to trust the one while we wait for the other.
manader.ingress: In February the light comes back in earnest, long before the warmth. It glitters on the snow crust, is heard in the birches and seen in the cottage windows, where the first seeds are already in the soil.

manader.sub: The sap rises, the ice lets go and Easter comes early
natur: March is the month when the migrant birds begin to come back, and most are heard before they are seen. The skylark usually arrives in early or mid-March and rises singing over the fields, so high it becomes a speck against the sky. The lapwing comes at about the same time, with its tumbling flights and plaintive pee-wit. The greylag geese fly in over Ekoln in pairs, and where the ice has opened the goldeneye drakes display with their heads thrown back against their backs. At the end of the month, often on a clear and windy day, the cranes’ trumpeting is heard long before the skein comes into view. A little later the curlew usually arrives, and its bubbling song flight is one of the loveliest sounds of spring.

Among the birds that have stayed all winter there is also new life. The blackbird begins to sing from the roof ridge at dusk, slow and flute-like. The great tits have settled on a nest box and are carrying in moss. The buzzard returns and circles over the meadow on broad wings, and by the end of the month the robin and the dunnock are usually in place in the thickets around the compost.

The first yellow appears in the ditches. Coltsfoot opens on bare soil in sunny spots, at the roadside and by the entrance, often while snow still lies in the shade. Hepaticas usually come at the end of March or in April on the slopes of the broadleaf woods. The goat willow has its silvery buds, the pussy willows, but flowers only in April. We leave it be. When the bumblebee queens wake, the goat willow is their first and most important food, and we would rather cut our Easter twigs from birch.

Under the bark more happens than meets the eye. When the frost begins to leave the ground and the days are mild, the birch’s roots draw water from the soil, and the sap rises in the trunk with sugar from the tree’s winter store. Whoever breaks a birch twig on such a day sees that it drips. That is what has given the Sap Moon its name. The sap usually flows from the end of March and through April, as long as the buds are closed, and it stops when the leaves begin to break. A small hole in a large birch can give several litres a day. We tap only large, healthy trees, for a few days per tree, and put a wooden plug in the hole afterwards.
karaktar: March often begins as winter and ends as spring, but the road between is seldom straight. One week the snow melts so that every ditch babbles, the next the fresh snow lies over the cold frames again. What does not change is the light. The day now grows faster than at any other time of year, by more than five minutes a day, and when the spring equinox comes on 20 March the day is already a little longer than the night. At the end of the month the clocks change to summer time, and suddenly it is light until half past seven in the evening.

At Vreta the start of spring shows first in the greenhouse. The chillies and sweet peppers from February have their first true leaves and are moved to larger pots, and new seed trays are filled every week: tomatoes, brassicas, lettuce, summer flowers for cutting. The cold frames by the cottage get a bed of fresh horse manure under the soil, which warms from below as it breaks down, and under the old windows the first radishes and lettuce can be sown. In the orangery the doors stand open for a while in the middle of sunny days, and the lemon trees put out new, pale-green shoots.

Outside it is still mostly waiting. The clay is heavy and wet after the snowmelt, and whoever walks on the beds now compacts it for the whole season – we keep to the paths. The pond still lies under ever thinner and greyer ice, and when it lets go the frogs come. In the forest garden the trees wake from the roots upwards. The last winter pruning of the apple trees is done before the buds begin to swell, and in the birches the sap rises long before anything green shows.

We call the month’s full moon the Sap Moon. It is full on Monday 22 March at 11.43, the same day as the Hindu spring festival Holi, and is seen best on the evenings before and after, when it rises in the east around sunset. It is also the Easter moon. By the old rule Easter is celebrated on the Sunday after the first full moon after the spring equinox, and this year it all falls close together: equinox on the Saturday, full moon on the Monday and Easter Day the following Sunday.
himmel: The spring equinox occurs on Saturday 20 March at 21.24. The sun then crosses the celestial equator heading north, and that day it rises almost due east and sets almost due west. Even so, day and night are not exactly the same length. Because the atmosphere bends the light and the sun is a disc and not a point, the day in Uppsala has already been longer than the night for a few days. We mark the place where the sun sets at the equinox with a stone at the meadow’s edge. It is one of the site journal’s photo points, and the same stone is used again in September.

The Sap Moon is full in the middle of the day on 22 March. It rises at 17.07 the evening before and at 18.44 the same evening, a good half hour after sunset, large and yellow in the east. On 8 March the moon is new, and late on the evening of Saturday 13 March the thin crescent slides in front of the Pleiades low in the west-north-west. With binoculars you can see some of the stars vanish one after another behind the moon’s dark edge, around 23.00.
citat: The sap rises before anyone sees it. Most of what grows does so in silence.
manader.ingress: March is the month when winter lets go without promising anything. The sap rises in the birches, the skylark sings over the fields and Easter falls in the last week of the month.

8 B’atz’ in the Maya calendar, when the K’iche’ Maya’s sacred 260-day calendar is traditionally celebrated and new daykeepers are initiated. We are not daykeepers, but we let the day remind us of time as a thread that goes on being spun.

At 21.24 the sun crosses the celestial equator heading north, and spring begins astronomically. The sun rises almost due east and sets almost due west.

The Easter witches (påskkärringar) go round with their Easter cards. It is also Waffle Day, the old Lady Day.

Eggs, herring and Easter twigs. In Uppland the bonfires belong to Walpurgis Night, but in western Sweden Easter fires are lit tonight.

The ice rots from within, and whoever walks out on it now takes a great risk. In the open leads along the shores whooper swans and goldeneyes gather, and the goldeneyes’ wings whistle as they fly past.
The fens
Meltwater fills the fens. Lapwings and the first gulls come back, and at the end of the month the black-headed gulls may begin to gather at Dalkarlskärret.
The tarn
The tarn thaws first of all the waters. In a warm week at the end of the month the first frogs may wake and make their way there.
The pond
The ice edge lets go of the granite boulders, and the water rises with meltwater. We check that the ditch and the overflow run freely.
events: On 8 B’atz’ we gather in the sewing room for an evening with spinning wheel, weaving frame and mending. B’atz’ is the thread in the Maya calendar, and the evening is about time that goes on being spun. Tea and conversation, no ceremony.
A course day on building a hotbed of horse manure, leaves and soil under old windows. In the evening we go out into the meadow with binoculars and watch the crescent moon slide into the Pleiades.

We follow the sunset from the stone at the meadow’s edge and light the fire at the fire place. At 21.24, when the equinox occurs, there is a minute’s silence. Guests who celebrate Nowruz are welcome to lay their haft-sin table in the orangery.
If the sap has begun to rise, we drill the first hole in one of the big birches and taste the sap at the long table. If it has not, we wait, and then the moon has to be enough.
An afternoon in the studio for children and families: we paint eggs, bind Easter twigs of birch and hang up wooden eggs from the joinery. Waffles in the orangery – Easter witches especially welcome.

The spirit hall stands open all day for anyone who wants to be in stillness, and a simple soup is made in the kitchen. Whoever keeps Good Friday as a Christian holy day does so, and whoever simply needs a quiet day has one.
We meet by the pond as the sun rises, just before half past six by the new summer time, and go on to Easter breakfast in the orangery. An egg hunt in the forest garden for the children.
Mornings for children during the Easter holiday: sowing in the greenhouse, pots of their own in the ceramics workshop and birdwatching by the pond once the ice has gone.

manader.sub: Frog song, the tipi and the Walpurgis bonfire
natur: The frogs often begin spawning only a few days after the ice has gone. The common frog is first. On the first mild, ideally rainy, evenings it migrates from the woods and the compost down to the pond, sometimes straight across the path. The males’ song is a low, soft purring heard best at dusk. Where the moor frog lives it sounds different, like air bubbles rising from a bottle under water, and its males can shimmer blue for a few days of the spawning. The spawn is laid in clumps in the shallow, sun-warmed water. The toads spawn somewhat later and lay their spawn in long strings around the water plants.

The pond quickly fills with other life too. The smaller newts come back from land to breed, the pond skaters walk on the surface again and in the mud on the bottom the dragonfly larvae move, having lived there for one or more years. On a warm afternoon the grass snake lies on its stone by the shore warming itself after the winter. It is harmless and protected, and it belongs to the pond as much as the frogs – which, incidentally, it is happy to eat.

The goat willow flowers in April, and it is the most important tree of spring for insects. The male trees glow yellow with pollen, the female trees are green and less conspicuous, and on a sunny day both hum. The bumblebee queens have woken from hibernation and need nectar and pollen quickly to start their colonies, and the goat willow is often all there is to be had. The bees from the hives at the meadow’s edge find their way there on the same days. The brimstone, the small tortoiseshell and the Camberwell beauty, which have all overwintered as adult butterflies, fly in the sunny clearings and seek out the same flowers.

On the ground the flowers come in quick succession. The coltsfoot finishes, the hepaticas glow on the slopes of the broadleaf woods and at the end of the month the wood anemones usually spread out under the trees. In the forest garden the rhubarb pushes up its crumpled red buds, the comfrey puts out its first leaves and the berry bushes, especially the gooseberries, come into leaf before almost anything else. The birch waits longest. The leaves usually break at the end of April or in early May, and when they are the size of mouse ears it is, by an old rule of thumb, time to sow.
karaktar: April is the month when Vreta goes from waiting to growing. It can still snow, and the frosty nights continue well into May, but the ground has begun to breathe. The frost leaves the soil, the ditches babble and the clay dries slowly from the surface. One morning the air is full of birdsong that was not there the week before, and towards the end of the month the birches gain a green shimmer that is hard to see up close but clear at a distance. The day is now several hours longer than the night, and on Walpurgis Night the sun does not set until a quarter to nine.

What has been prepared over the winter now comes out. The tipi is carried out of the store and raised in the meadow. The outdoor kitchen and the bar of granite and limestone are cleaned, and the long table under the old oak receives its first guests on a sunny afternoon. The plants from the greenhouse are moved out to the cold frames to harden off, and the first seeds are sown directly in the open ground when the soil crumbles in the hand. By the gate the café and the shop are prepared for the season’s opening on the weekend of 1–2 May.

The pond is nonetheless the centre of April. When the ice has gone and the first mild nights come, the frogs gather in the shallow water along the sun-warmed granite boulders. For a few intense days and nights they spawn, sing and lay their spawn, and then it is quiet again. It is one of the year’s short and self-evident festivals. It comes every spring, and it is over before one has had time to get used to it.

We call the month’s full moon the Frog Moon. It is full at 00.27 in the night between Tuesday 20 and Wednesday 21 April. It rises just after sunset and stands low in the south all night, so low that it can be mirrored in the pond between the birch trunks. It is also the first full moon we welcome in the tipi this season.
himmel: The Frog Moon is full at 00.27 in the night before Wednesday 21 April. It rises at 20.27, only a few minutes after sunset, and then stands low over the treetops in the south all night. Spring full moons always run low at our latitudes, since they stand opposite a sun that is climbing towards summer. The following night, 22 April, the Lyrids reach their maximum. It is an old and reliable meteor shower, but this year the moon is almost full and washes out most of the shooting stars.

Jupiter is still the brightest light of the evening and stands high in the south as it grows dark. Mars shines beside it but ever paler, and during the month it fades to about the same brightness as the brightest stars. On the evening of 15 April the waxing moon stands close to them both. Venus is formally a morning star but stands so close to the sun at dawn that it can hardly be seen from our latitudes. High overhead stands the Plough, and whoever follows the arc of its handle comes to Arcturus, the orange star in Boötes, and on to Spica in Virgo.
citat: The frogs do not ask whether spring has come. They sing until it does.
manader.ingress: In April the pond wakes. The frogs sing at dusk, the goat willow turns yellow with pollen and the tipi is raised again in the meadow.

A meteor shower that has been observed for more than 2,500 years. This year the moon is almost full and washes out most of the shooting stars.

The great evening of spring. In Uppsala there is rafting down the Fyris river, the donning of student caps at 15.00 outside Carolina Rediviva and bonfires in the evening – this year during the university’s jubilee year. It is also the King’s birthday and a general flag day.

The ice often breaks up in April. The pike spawns soon after, in shallow bays and flooded reed beds such as Dalbyviken, and the perch follows as the water grows warmer. The osprey comes back and the goldeneye displays. Lake Mälaren’s water level is on average at its highest in April.
The fens

The bittern begins to boom in the reeds around Dalbyviken, a deep sound that carries far at dusk. The grebes come back, the black-headed gull colony at Dalkarlskärret fills and the marsh harrier glides low over the reeds.
The tarn
The frogs are spawning. The clumps of spawn lie in the shallow, sun-warmed water, and the toads make their way there at dusk. Walk carefully on the path on a mild, damp evening.
The pond

A shared day to make the place ready for the season. Lunch at the long table.

Whoever wishes goes into Uppsala for the donning of the caps at 15.00. In the evening the Walpurgis bonfire is lit in the meadow, we sing in the spring and eat soup by the tipi. The bonfire is restacked the same day, so that no animals have had time to move in.

manader.sub: Gökotta, blossom and the last frost
natur: The cuckoo usually arrives in the first week of May. It is heard long before it is seen, and many never hear it as more than an echo from the edge of the woods. In folk belief it mattered from which direction you first heard it: from east and west it meant comfort and happiness, from the north sorrow and from the south death. We listen mostly to know that it is back. At about the same time the thrush nightingale begins to sing in the leafy thickets around Ekoln – a stream of clear whistles, rattling trills and long pauses, in the middle of the night when nearly all other birds have fallen silent. Around 15–20 May the swifts arrive. They are among the last migrants to come and among the first to leave us.

The blossom goes quickly. The bird cherry opens in mid- or late May, and its scent draws flies, bees and bumblebees. Some years the caterpillars of the bird-cherry ermine then wrap the bushes in silvery-white webs. It looks dramatic, but the bird cherry usually comes into leaf again. The apple trees blossom at the end of the month, often with the lilac hedge along the road close behind. Under the trees the dandelions glow. They are one of the most important larders of spring for bees and bumblebees, and so they are allowed to finish flowering before we mow the paths in the grass.

Further into the forest garden the currants and gooseberries have already flowered, with small yellow-green flowers that are easy to miss but that the bumblebees find. With the warmth come the aphids, and soon after them the ladybirds, hoverflies and lacewings. We spray nothing. It takes a few weeks for the balance to settle, and meanwhile some shoots may look a little battered. That is the price of a garden where birds and insects do much of the work.

In the forest garden and along the ditches stand the wild vegetables of spring. Nettles are best when young, and it is the tops that are picked – with gloves. Ground elder, which many gardeners fight, is a mild and good leaf vegetable before it flowers. Ramsons thrive in the damp shade and flower towards the end of the month. They should be picked with care, since the leaves resemble those of lily of the valley, and lily of the valley is poisonous. We always leave one nettle patch untouched. There the small tortoiseshell and the peacock lay their eggs, and the caterpillars live only on nettles.
karaktar: May is the month when Vreta opens its gate in earnest. On the first weekend the tables are carried out onto the gravel in front of the farmhouse, the parasols go up and the café and the shop open for the season. The plants from the greenhouse stand in rows on the old cart with the wooden wheels, and whoever comes for a cup of coffee often goes home with a tomato plant under their arm. Now the guests begin to come. The rooms fill at weekends, and the workshops move out onto the yard as soon as the weather allows.

Meanwhile most of it happens without us. The birches go from mouse ears to full leaf in a couple of weeks. The bird cherry flowers and lays its sweet, almost heavy scent over the pond, and at the end of the month the apple trees open in the forest garden. The cuckoo calls from the woodland edge, the thrush nightingale sings in the thickets down towards Ekoln and the bees work every flower that is open. It is hard to be indoors in May, and we do not try.

But May has a catch. The nights can still turn cold, and on a clear, still night the frost can take whatever was planted out too early. So the tomatoes, courgettes and beans stay in the greenhouse and cold frames a while longer. They are hardened off in sun and wind by day and brought in or covered at night. In folk belief Cold Sophie, 15 May, is the last frost night of the year. It is no rule, but it is a good reminder for anyone in a hurry.

The light grows by several minutes each day. On 1 May the sun rises at 04.46 and on 31 May as early as 03.38. From the middle of the month it never gets truly dark, and the northern sky keeps a pale glow all night. We call the month’s full moon the Nettle Moon, after the plant that now shoots up in every nitrogen-rich corner of the place – and is the most underrated vegetable of spring. It is full on Thursday 20 May, the same day as Vesak.
himmel: The May sky is light. From around 12 May the sun does not sink even twelve degrees below the horizon, the night never grows truly dark, and the stars fade away in a blue dusk that runs straight into dawn. What can be seen is the brightest. Jupiter and Mars remain in Leo in the west-south-west in the evenings, but they drift apart and sink with every week. On the evening of 12 May the waxing moon stands right beside Jupiter, and the next evening beside Mars and Regulus. Venus cannot be seen – it is too close to the sun.

The new moon on 6 May and the full moon on 20 May occur at the same time of day, 12.58. The Nettle Moon rises just before 23.00 far down in the south-south-east and never reaches more than a few degrees above the horizon in the south. Summer full moons always stand low, since they lie opposite the high summer sun. It is seen best where the horizon is clear, and on a hazy evening it can glow almost orange as it lifts above the trees.
citat: In May the hardest work is waiting.
manader.ingress: In May everything wakes at once. The art is to find time to see it – and to wait with whatever cannot stand frost.

dates: The day of the labour movement, a public holiday since 1939 and a general flag day. The same day the café and the shop open for the season.
The Orthodox churches calculate Easter by the Julian calendar, and this year it falls five weeks after the Western one. Red-dyed eggs belong to the celebration.
A public holiday and the traditional day for gökotta – going out at dawn to listen to the birds, and with a little luck the cuckoo. The moon is new at 12.58.
On the evening of 12 May the waxing moon stands right beside Jupiter in the west-south-west. The next evening it has moved to Mars and Regulus, the brightest star in Leo.
By folk belief the last frost night of the year. No guarantee – but whoever waits until after Sophie with the frost-tender plants has seldom regretted it.
A public holiday and flag day. The Swedish name, pingst, comes from the Greek word for the fiftieth, and the festival falls on the fiftieth day counting from Easter Day.

The Festival of Sacrifice, one of the two great festivals of Islam, in memory of Ibrahim’s – Abraham’s – willingness to sacrifice. Celebrated with prayer, a shared meal and gifts to those in need. The exact date depends on when the crescent moon is seen.
The Buddha’s birth, enlightenment and passing are celebrated in many countries at the full moon in May. The moon is full at 12.58. The same day is the UN’s World Bee Day.
The UN’s international day for biodiversity. A good reason to count the species in the meadow, the pond and the forest garden.
Celebrated in Sweden on the last Sunday in May. The café opens early for breakfast under the blossoming apple trees.
water: Ekoln

The roach spawn on shallow shores, and when the water has reached about ten degrees the zander spawn on hard bottoms, where the male guards the nest. Show consideration during spawning and follow the fishing rules. The common terns are back, and the great crested grebes display with their crests raised.
The fens
The fens are at their liveliest. The black-headed gulls shriek in the colony, the little grebe and the whooper swan breed in Stora kärret, and sedge warblers and reed warblers sing in the reeds.
The tarn
The tarn teems with tadpoles. The first dragonfly larvae climb up the stems and emerge.
The pond
We plant new water plants in the pond’s shallow zone. The grass snake suns itself on the granite boulders, and the female newts lay their eggs one by one, each wrapped in a leaf.
events: The café and the shop open for the season. Plants from the greenhouse are sold on the gravel, and by the old cart we swap cuttings, perennials and seeds with neighbours and guests. Rhubarb cake and coffee at the outdoor tables.

We gather at the gate at 04.15, just before sunrise, and walk in silence through the forest garden to the meadow. There we listen, with flasks and blankets. Breakfast at the long table when the birds have finished singing.

A course on the wild vegetables of spring: nettle, ground elder, ramsons and dandelion. We pick in the forest garden and along the ditches, make soup and pesto in the outdoor kitchen and brew nettle feed for the garden. Children welcome with an adult.

A morning at the meadow’s edge with an experienced beekeeper. We look into a hive, learn to recognise queen cells and talk about swarming, honey and wild bees. Suits and veils are available to borrow. Anyone allergic to bee stings takes part at a distance.

A quiet evening in the spirit hall with candles and meditation, ideally led by Buddhists from the area who wish to share their festival with us. Afterwards we walk down towards Ekoln to see whether the full moon shows as it rises low in the south-south-east.

The risk of frost is past in most years. The tomatoes are planted in the greenhouse, courgettes, beans and sweetcorn in the open ground under fleece for the first nights, and the citrus trees are carried out of the orangery. Shared dinner at the long table on Saturday evening.
The café opens early for breakfast at the outdoor tables and under the apple trees: bread from the wood-fired oven, eggs from the hens and rhubarb compote. Book in advance.

Lie still in tall grass from the end of May. Do not touch them – the mother is never far away.
Ramsons and lily of the valley
The leaves look alike, and lily of the valley is poisonous. Ramsons smell of garlic, but the scent clings to your fingers – pick leaf by leaf and look closely.
Tawny owl chicks
Fluffy young sitting on branches near the nest box in the old oak. Do not go too close – the tawny owl defends its young.
Ticks
Become active in grass and scrub. Check your body after a day in the meadow and remove any tick with tweezers as early as possible.
The bird cherry
Flowers in mid- to late May. Later the bird-cherry ermine’s webs may cover the bushes – leave them, the bird cherry will cope.
manader.hand: Wait for Sophie. Listen for the cuckoo.

natur: The meadow is at its richest now. The ox-eye daisies glow white over the grass, the buttercups yellow, and the red clover and tufted vetch draw in bumblebees with long tongues. The harebells come somewhat later and flower well into summer. A meadow is not a flower bed but a community, and every year it looks a little different – species come and go depending on the spring, the rain and last year’s mowing. We walk through it on the mown paths and leave the rest standing. The mowing must wait until the flowers have set seed.

Early summer has its own scents. At the beginning of June the lilac hedge along the road finishes flowering, and whoever comes in through the gate walks through a cloud of lilac. In the shade under the trees the lilies of the valley flower – lovely to look at but poisonous, and nothing to pick for the kitchen. At the woodland edge the violet flowers of the wood cranesbill glow. And in the evenings, when the air is still, the meadow smells of honey far out across the gravel.

The elder bushes flower in mid- and late June, with flat, creamy-white flower heads that smell of honey and muscatel. It is the black elder we pick for cordial. The red-berried elder, which flowered as early as May and bears red berries, we leave alone. The flowers are picked on a sunny morning when they are fully open and full of pollen, and they are not rinsed – the flavour is in the pollen. At the end of the month the wild strawberries redden along the edges of the forest garden, and the first strawberries ripen on the straw.

There are young birds everywhere. Some are still in the nest boxes begging loudly, others have left the nest before they can fly properly and hop about in the grass. They have seldom got lost. The parents feed them nearby, and the best we can do is to leave them alone and keep the cats away. The swallows hunt over the pond, the swifts scream over the roofs and the cuckoo still calls, but falls silent towards the end of the month.
karaktar: June is Vreta’s liveliest month. After the end of the school year the café and the shop switch to summer opening hours and are open several days a week. The outdoor kitchen and the bar are the hub of the place. That is where the food is cooked, where the washing-up is done and where people stand talking long after they really meant to leave.

The meadow is in full bloom. Ox-eye daisies, buttercups, red clover, tufted vetch and harebells form a patchwork that changes from week to week, and it hums with bumblebees and bees. The elder bushes open in the middle of the month, the first wild strawberries redden along the edges and in the greenhouse the tomatoes set their first trusses. The work moves to mornings and evenings. In the middle of the day, when it is hottest, we rest in the shade under the oak.

On 21 June at 16.10 the sun turns. It is the longest day of the year, with almost nineteen hours between sunrise and sunset. The sun sets in the north-west just after 22.00, lingers a little over five hours below the horizon and rises again in the north-east. At midnight it stands only a little over six degrees below the horizon, and it never grows darker than a deep twilight.

We call the month’s full moon the Bright Moon. The name is a paradox, for this particular moon is hard to see. It is full in the night before Saturday 19 June and barely lifts above the horizon in the south. It is the night itself that is bright in June. The moon has to be content with being a pale guest in it.
himmel: June is the lightest month of the year. At the solstice the sun rises at 03.23 and sets at 22.19, and at midnight it lies only a little over six degrees below the horizon in the north. The sky never grows darker than a deep, blue twilight, and only the brightest stars show: Vega high in the south, Arcturus in the west-south-west and Capella low in the north. Jupiter stands low in the west after sunset and slowly disappears into the evening light. On the evenings of 9 and 10 June a waxing crescent passes Jupiter, Regulus and Mars, but in the light sky only Jupiter shows clearly.

The Bright Moon is full at 02.44 in the night before Saturday 19 June. It rises just before 23.00 the evening before, far down in the south-south-east, reaches barely three degrees above the horizon just before 01.00 and sets in the south-west at about the time it becomes full. It is the lowest full moon of the year. From Vreta the trees can easily hide it entirely, and you need a clear view to the south to see it at all. If it does show, it is often large, yellow-red and strangely flattened near the horizon.
citat: In June evening and morning meet without the night finding room between them.
manader.ingress: In June the night almost runs out. The sun sets in the north-west, lingers a few hours below the horizon and rises again in the north-east.
stat: 18 h 53 min
of daylight on 15 June in Uppsala. Around the solstice there are a few minutes more – then the days begin to shrink.
dates: A public holiday and the day of the Swedish flag. Gustav Vasa was elected king on 6 June 1523, and on the same date in 1809 a new Instrument of Government was adopted.
Around this day the year 1449 after the Hijra begins, with the first crescent after the new moon on 4 June. The new year is usually marked quietly.
Uppsala’s schools end the spring term. The summer holidays begin, and the café and the shop switch to summer opening hours.
The Jewish Feast of Weeks, seven weeks after Passover, in memory of the giving of the Torah at Sinai. Begins at sunset the evening before. Dairy food and the year’s first fruits belong to it.
Full moon at 02.44, in the night between Friday and Saturday. The lowest full moon of the year – it reaches only a couple of degrees above the horizon in the south.
The sun turns at 16.10. The same day the Aymara people of the Andes celebrate their new year, Willkakuti – in the southern hemisphere it is the winter solstice, and the sun begins to return.
Inti Raymi and St John’s Day
The Inca festival of the sun, revived in Cusco since the mid-twentieth century. In the Christian calendar it is the day of John the Baptist – until 1953 also the Swedish Midsummer Day.

Not a public holiday in the legal sense, but the year’s greatest day of celebration for many Swedes. The maypole is dressed and raised, and the evening belongs to herring, new potatoes and strawberries.
A public holiday and flag day. In the Maya calendar it is 13 Ajpu, the last day of the sacred count of 260 days. Ajpu is often associated with the sun.
The Maya calendar’s count begins again with 1 Imox, a day associated with water. By folk belief, if it rains on Seven Sleepers’ Day it will rain for seven weeks.
water: Ekoln

Bream and zander spawn, and the bream spawning can be heard as splashing in the reeds. The water grows warm enough for the first real swim around Midsummer. In the deeper parts of the bay a warm layer settles over the cold.
The fens
The grebe chicks ride on their parents’ backs, and the swans swim with their grey cygnets. The bittern falls silent towards the end of the month.
The tarn
The tadpoles grow legs, and towards the end of June the little frogs leave the water. Do not cut the grass around the tarn now.
The pond
The dragonflies emerge and the damselflies dance over the water. If the water drops we top it up with rainwater from the butts, never with tap water.
events: Walks through the forest garden, the meadow, the ponds and the workshops, led by those who tend them. Coffee at the outdoor tables and the flag flying at the gate. Open to all.
The first swim of the summer holidays

On the evening after the end of the school year the sauna is fired and the bathing steps are opened for children and adults together. An adult always stays on land keeping watch. Cordial and buns on the stones by the pond afterwards.
We walk slowly through the meadow with a flora and a loupe, count the species and press a few flowers for the site journal. On Sunday botanical drawing and watercolour in the studio. For all ages.
The night of the Bright Moon

A night walk down towards Ekoln to try to see the full moon, which rises low in the south-south-east just before 23.00 and barely lifts above the treetops. We finish with the sauna and a while in silence by the pond.
Elderflower weekend in the outdoor kitchen
We pick elderflowers on a sunny morning and set cordial and elderflower drink in large glass jars. Everything steeps for a day or two before it is strained. Recipes and a bottle to take home.

When the sun turns at 16.10 we strike a single beat on one of the drums in the spirit hall. In the evening we gather in the meadow and follow the sun down in the north-west at 22.19, in silence. A small fire in the tipi if the fire risk allows.

In the morning we bind crowns and dress the maypole with birch twigs and meadow flowers. The pole is raised in the afternoon and we dance around it. Herring, new potatoes and strawberries at the long table under the oak, and late in the evening we walk through the woods down to the jetty on Ekoln. Booking in advance.

13 Ajpu and 1 Imox. An evening in the spirit hall about what has been completed, and an early morning by the pond about what is beginning. Inspired by the Maya calendar, with no claim to be anything else.

watch: Noctilucent clouds
Silvery-blue, veined clouds low in the north around midnight from mid-June. They lie about 80 kilometres up and are lit by a sun that has already set.
Glow-worms
Small green points of light in the grass on warm, still evenings. It is the females that glow to attract the males.
Young birds on the ground
Young that have left the nest but cannot yet fly properly. Leave them be – the parents feed them nearby.
Elderflowers
Flat, creamy-white flower heads in mid- to late June. Pick black elder on a sunny morning and do not rinse the flowers.
Bee swarms
The swarming season runs into June. A cluster in a tree means the beekeeper should be called, not that anyone should go closer.
Grass snake eggs
Leathery white eggs in the compost from the end of June. Leave the compost until they have hatched at the end of summer.
Thunder
Get out of the water and into a house when thunder approaches. Three seconds between flash and bang is roughly a kilometre.
Ticks
Check your body every evening. A redness that spreads around a bite should be shown to a doctor, and there is a vaccine against TBE, which occurs in the area.
The Bright Moon
In the night between 18 and 19 June the full moon stands only a couple of degrees above the horizon in the south. It takes a clear view – and luck.

manader.sub: The scythe, the berries and the honey
natur: The meadow changes colour in July. The ox-eye daisies and buttercups finish flowering, and in their place come knapweed, lady’s bedstraw, St John’s wort, bird’s-foot trefoil and yarrow. The bumblebees work the clover and the knapweed from early morning, and the butterflies – brimstones, peacocks and fritillaries – gather on the violet flowers. Where yellow rattle has taken hold, it is the meadow’s own clock. When the seeds rattle in the dry seed pods it is time to mow.

At the beginning of July the limes in the area flower, and their scent is so sweet it can be sensed long before the trees are seen. Bees love lime, and whoever stands under a flowering lime on a warm afternoon hears the whole crown hum. Along the ditches the rosebay willowherb opens in pink, and at the edges of the forest garden the comfrey’s hanging bells draw the bumblebees from morning to evening.

It is the month of berries. In the forest garden the currants, gooseberries and raspberries ripen, and the wild strawberries go on giving under the bushes. Out in the forests the bilberries ripen from early or mid-July. The right of public access (allemansrätten) gives everyone the right to pick berries and mushrooms in forest and field, but not close to anyone’s house and garden. After a few days of rain the chanterelles appear in mossy mixed woodland. Whoever picks mushrooms takes only what they know for certain, and whoever is unsure leaves them.

The birdsong falls silent. Once the young have left the nests most birds stop singing and begin to moult, and the woods grow strangely still. The barn swallows lay a second clutch, and the young from the first sit in rows on the wires. At the end of July or the beginning of August the swifts leave us. One evening the sky over the roofs is suddenly silent, and then you know that summer has passed its height.
karaktar: July is the holiday month, and Vreta is full of people. The days begin early with a swim in the pond and end late at the long table. In the middle of the day, when the heat lies heavy over the meadow, we do as people have always done in the country: we rest in the shade and make up the work in the evening.

It is also the beginning of the harvest. New potatoes, peas and the first beans come from the open ground, the courgettes grow faster than anyone can eat them and in the greenhouse the first tomatoes ripen towards the end of the month. In the forest garden the currants hang in heavy strings, the raspberries ripen and the wild strawberries keep giving, a few berries at a time. The bees fill the honey supers, and after a couple of days of rain the chanterelles may come in the surrounding woods. The cottage kitchen and the outdoor kitchen run at full tilt with cordial, jam and pickles.

At the end of the month comes the mowing. The meadow has finished flowering and the flowers have set seed, and now it is cut with a scythe, in stages, so that something is always left standing for the insects. The hay dries on racks and is then carried away. That is how the meadow is kept lean and rich in species, and that is how meadows have been tended for hundreds of years. We call the month’s full moon the Haymaking Moon. It is full on Sunday 18 July.

The light has turned, but it shows only late. During the first weeks the nights are almost as light as in June. Then it goes quickly. On 31 July the sun sets at 21.24, almost an hour earlier than at Midsummer, and around midnight it grows dim enough, for the first time since May, for the brightest stars to show again.
himmel: During July the darkness slowly comes back. At the beginning of the month the nights are almost as light as at Midsummer, but on 31 July the sun sinks almost twelve degrees below the horizon at midnight, and the sky has time to turn deep blue. The brightest stars show again. Deneb stands high overhead, Vega high in the south-west and Altair in the south – together they form the Summer Triangle. Arcturus shines low in the west. Noctilucent clouds can still glow low in the north around midnight until early August.

The Haymaking Moon is full at 17.44 on Sunday 18 July. A very faint penumbral eclipse occurs around 18.00, when the moon just grazes the edge of the earth’s penumbra. It cannot be seen from Uppsala – the moon has not yet risen, and the eclipse is so faint it is barely noticeable anywhere. The moon rises in the south-east around 22.00, just after sunset, and travels low across the southern sky all night.
citat: The scythe takes only what has already given its seed.
manader.ingress: In July summer stands still for a while. Then, almost imperceptibly, it begins to lean towards autumn.
stat: 18 h 47 min
of daylight on 1 July in Uppsala. On 31 July the day is 16 h 59 min – almost two hours shorter in a month.
dates: The moon is new at 05.01. The Haymaking Moon’s round begins, but on the first evenings the crescent is too thin and too low to be seen in the light sky.
A general flag day. This year the Crown Princess turns fifty.
Around now the earth begins to pass through the Perseid meteor stream. So far there are only occasional shooting stars in the light nights – the maximum comes on the night of 12–13 August.
Full moon at 17.44. A very faint penumbral eclipse occurs around 18.00, before the moon has risen here. The moon rises just after sunset, around 22.00.

By folk belief they last until 23 August, a time when food spoils and wounds heal badly. They are also called the dog days after Sirius, the Dog Star, which in antiquity rose with the sun at this time.
"St James drops a cold stone in the lake." The water is said to begin cooling now. At Vreta the last stretches of the meadow are cut, and the day ends with a haymaking feast.
The moon wanes and leaves the darkening nights to the stars. The Summer Triangle – Vega, Deneb and Altair – stands high in the south around midnight.
In memory of Olaf the Holy, who fell at Stiklestad in 1030. In Norway the day is called Olsok, and in the Faroe Islands Ólavsøka is the national day.
water: Ekoln

The surface water is at its warmest at the end of July and the beginning of August. Warm, still days can bring algal bloom – a green or yellow-green layer with flakes. Do not swim then, and do not let the dog drink. The osprey chicks fledge.
The fens
The ducks moult in the shelter of the reeds and cannot fly for a few weeks. The fens are quiet and green.
The tarn
The tarn can shrink in a dry summer. That is natural, and it fills again with the autumn rains.
The pond
Blanket weed can spread. We lift some of it out with a rake and lay it on the edge for a day, so that small creatures can crawl back into the water.
events: Five days of whittling, throwing, smithing and sewing for adults and young people. Mornings in the workshops, afternoons by the pond and lunch at the long table.
Red and blackcurrants are picked in the forest garden and become cordial and jelly in the outdoor kitchen. We fill jars for the larder and the shop, and everyone takes a bottle home.

We show how a frame is uncapped and extracted in a closed room the bees cannot reach, taste honey straight from the comb and talk about varroa and the wild bees. The new honey is sold in the shop the same day.
Long table under the Haymaking Moon

A slow dinner of July’s harvest under the apple tree, with lanterns on the table. When the moon rises in the south-east around 22.00 we walk a little way into the meadow and watch it lift above the trees.

The meadow is cut with a scythe in stages once the flowers have set seed. We show how the scythe is peened and sharpened, rake and rack the hay and finish with a haymaking feast at the long table on St James’s Day. Sturdy shoes and plenty of distance between those mowing.
The darkness has begun to come back, and for the first time since May the lanterns are needed. Tales and stories for children and adults in the tipi, with sheepskins on the floor.

A morning in the woods of the area with a knowledgeable guide. We learn to recognise the chanterelle and tell it from its look-alikes, and fry the catch in the outdoor kitchen. Only what we know for certain goes home with us.

watch: Yellow rattle
When the seeds rattle in the dry pods the meadow is ready for mowing. An old sign that still works.
The ants’ nuptial flight
On a warm, humid afternoon winged ants rise from every anthill at once. The swallows and swifts know all about it.
Chanterelles
Often appear after a few days of rain in mossy mixed woodland. Pick only what you know for certain.
The swifts’ departure
One evening at the end of July or the beginning of August the sky over the roofs is suddenly silent. Note the date.
Blue-green algae

Wasps
Grow more numerous at the end of July. Cover cordial and jam outdoors and look in your glass before you drink.
The hawker’s larval skin

manader.sub: Shooting stars, berries and the late-summer larder
natur: In August the birdsong falls silent. The swifts, which screamed over the farmhouse all summer, have mostly left us at the end of July or the beginning of August. The barn swallows are still feeding their late broods, but towards the end of the month they usually gather on the wires along the road, close in a row, before the journey south. Along the shores of Ekoln waders rest that are already on their way from the north – greenshanks, common sandpipers and woodcock searching for food at the wet water’s edge.

The forest and the forest garden ripen at the same time. The bilberries have been there since July, and at the end of August the lingonberries redden on the rocks and in the clearings of the pine woods. In the forest garden the last currants and gooseberries are picked. The elder’s berry clusters darken towards black – they must always be cooked before they are eaten. The rose hips turn red, and at the end of the month the first hazelnuts may come loose from their green husks. The first apples are summer apples, such as Transparente blanche. They are pale, tart and good straight from the tree, but they do not keep. After a few days they turn mealy, so they become purée the same week.

After rain come the mushrooms. The chanterelles have often been there since July, and in August ceps may appear at the woodland edge and under the birches. Mushroom picking takes knowledge. Never eat a mushroom you are not completely sure of, and better to pick a few kinds you know well than many you think you know.

The wasps are at their most numerous now. The colonies have grown all summer, and the workers seek out anything sweet – cordial glasses, jam bowls and windfalls. We cover the glasses in the café and do not drink from cans outdoors, and anyone who is allergic keeps their medicine close. Between the bushes the garden spiders stretch their great wheel webs. Over the pond the dragonflies still hunt in the sun. In the hives the drones’ time is over – at the end of summer the worker bees drive them out.
karaktar: August is the last and richest month of summer. The meadow is mown and the hay carried away, but the forest garden has never been heavier. The currant bushes lean with berries, the first summer apples fall into the grass and the hazel sets nuts in small clusters. In the kitchen the copper pan is on the stove almost every day.

But something has changed. The light has turned golden and lower, and the evenings end earlier. On 1 August the sun rises at 04.27 and sets at 21.22. On the last day of August it sets as early as 19.58. In a month the day loses more than two and a half hours, and after the middle of the month it grows completely dark in the middle of the night for the first time since April. The lanterns in the apple tree, lit again at the end of July, are now needed every evening.

The month has two halves. The first is still holiday, with families in the tipi and at the long table, swims in the pond and long afternoons in the café, which is open several days a week. The second begins when the schools open on 18 August. Then the weekdays grow calmer, and instead of the families come the course groups – to the kitchens, the workshops and the spirit hall. The weekends still belong to those who want a day of coffee, a swim and a sauna.

We call the month’s full moon the Berry Moon. It is full on Tuesday morning, 17 August, at 09.28, so it is on the evenings before and after that it shines round over the meadow. The August moon runs low, and it rises at almost the same time several evenings in a row – just after eight, while the sky is still light. The name says what the month is about: bilberries and lingonberries in the forest, currants and gooseberries in the forest garden, rose hips in the hedge and rowan berries beginning to glow orange.
himmel: The month begins with an unusual event. On Monday 2 August the moon passes in front of the sun. In Spain, North Africa and Egypt the eclipse is total – at Luxor for more than six minutes, and it has been called the eclipse of the century. In Uppsala we see only a small part of it. It begins at about 10.39, is greatest at about 11.19 and ends at about 12.00. At most the moon covers a little over a fifth of the sun’s diameter, about twelve per cent of its area, and the daylight barely changes. Never look directly at the sun, not even for a moment. Ordinary sunglasses do not protect, and binoculars or a camera without the right filter can damage the eye in an instant. Use approved eclipse glasses, or look indirectly through a small hole in a piece of card that casts an image of the sun onto white paper. Under a tree, the leaves do it by themselves.

On the night between Thursday 12 and Friday 13 August the Perseids reach their maximum. The shooting stars are fast and sometimes leave a glowing trail behind them. The moon sets at 23.30, and after midnight the sky is dark until dawn at around 03.30. The shooting stars seem to come from Perseus in the north-east, but they can appear across the whole sky, so the best thing is to lie down and look straight up. It is also now that the Milky Way becomes visible again, and the Summer Triangle – Vega, Deneb and Altair – stands high once it has grown dark.
citat: Whoever picks in August eats in February.
manader.ingress: In August the darkness comes back, and with it the stars. At the same time everything ripens at once, and in the kitchens the jam boils from morning to evening.

dates: In the Andes August is counted as the month of Pachamama, Mother Earth. It is then customary to give back to the earth – food, drink and thanks – before a new growing season. We invite those who carry the tradition, but we do not take it over.
Between about 10.39 and 12.00 the moon covers a small part of the sun, at most around 11.19. In Spain, North Africa and Egypt the eclipse is total. Never look directly at the sun.
At 12.05, the same morning as the eclipse. It is the new moon that makes the eclipse possible – the moon then stands between the earth and the sun.

Traditionally the first Wednesday in August. The day has its roots in the time when crayfishing was strictly regulated. Today it is mostly a reason to bring out dill crowns, paper lanterns and songbooks.
The most reliable meteor shower of the year. The moon sets at 23.30, and after midnight the sky is dark until dawn at around 03.30.

The autumn term begins in Uppsala’s schools. For many families it is the real boundary between summer and autumn.
The third Thursday in August. The tin is opened outdoors, ideally under water in a tub, and the fish is eaten with soft flatbread, almond potatoes and red onion.
In folk belief the dog days were reckoned from 23 July to 23 August – a time when food was thought to spoil quickly and the flies were many. Even so, it is now that we make jam.
The month’s second new moon, at 19.41. The evening is dark, and the late-summer starry sky stands clear once the twilight has passed.
water: Ekoln
The water cools slowly. The moon lays its path across the bay again, now that the nights are dark. The common terns leave, and the osprey fishes busily before migrating.
The fens

From 10.30 under the birches by the meadow. We lend approved eclipse glasses, build pinhole cameras from cardboard and follow the crescents on a white cloth. For all ages.
The café serves crayfish sandwiches and, for those who do not eat shellfish, chanterelle toast on sourdough. Dill crowns and paper lanterns are hung up for the month’s parties.

For those who want it – and at a suitable distance from those who do not. The tin is opened in a tub of water, and the fish is eaten with soft flatbread, almond potatoes, red onion and soured cream at the granite bar.

watch: The Perseids
Fast shooting stars after midnight on the night between 12 and 13 August. Lie down, give your eyes a quarter of an hour to adjust to the dark and look straight up.
Crescents under the birch
On the morning of 2 August the spots of light under the trees take the shape of small crescents. Look at the ground – never at the sun.
Swallows on the wire
Barn swallows gathering in long rows before migration. One morning at the end of August or in September they are gone.
The first lingonberries
Redden first on sunny rocks and in clearings. Wait until the berries are red all round.
Wasps at the cordial
Most numerous at the end of summer. Cover the glasses and look in your mug before you drink.
The garden spider’s web
Large wheel webs between the bushes, often rebuilt every night. Best seen in the morning dew.

manader.sub: Equinox, apple juice and the passage of the cranes
natur: September’s mightiest sound comes from the sky. In the middle and at the end of the month the cranes head south in long skeins, often so high that you hear them long before you see them. The geese follow, sometimes in their hundreds over Ekoln. The barn swallows leave us during September. Many small birds migrate at night, and whoever stands outside on a still evening can hear their thin calls high above.

The mornings are damp and still. The garden spiders’ webs hang between the grass stems and the tansy stalks, and when the dew settles they become visible everywhere. The first frost may come at the end of September, but it does not come everywhere at once. The first white morning usually shows in the hollows by the pond, where the cold air runs down and collects. In September or early October the meteorological autumn also arrives – when the average daily temperature stays below ten degrees for five days in a row.

Now the peak of the mushroom season begins. Ceps grow under spruce, pine and birch, the yellowfoot chanterelles begin to appear in the mossy spruce woods, and the brittlegills glow red, yellow and violet along the paths. Under the birches stand the first fly agarics. But with the quantity of mushrooms the risks grow too. The destroying angel, which is deadly poisonous, grows in the same woods as the good mushrooms. The deadly webcap can be mistaken for the yellowfoot, and its poison damages the kidneys, with symptoms that may appear only after several days. Never eat a mushroom you are not completely sure of, and learn the most poisonous first.

The trees begin to turn. The rowan is often first, with red leaves among the orange clusters of berries. Acorns fall from the old oak, and the hazelnuts ripen in the bushes – if the squirrels and jays do not get there first. The rose hips are dark red and soft, and the apple trees in the forest garden give most of the year’s harvest. In the forest the elk are in rut. They move about more than usual, also at dusk and across the roads.
karaktar: In September Vreta moves from growing to gathering in. The potatoes are lifted in the open ground, carrots and beetroot are laid in boxes of sand in the root cellar and the pumpkins lie in a row in the greenhouse to cure. The apple trees in the forest garden bow under their load, and the neighbours come with their surplus in buckets and sacks. In the kitchens there is a smell of mushrooms, apple purée and freshly pressed juice. It is the busiest month of the year in the larder – and one of the most generous.

The mornings have changed. The nights are cold while the water in the pond still holds the summer’s warmth, so mist often lies thick over the pond when we come out. On 1 September the sun rises at 05.41 and sets at 19.55. On 30 September it rises at 06.49 and sets as early as 18.28. Midway between, on Thursday 23 September at 08.01, is the autumn equinox. A few days later the night has grown longer than the day, and so it remains all the way to March.

The rhythm shifts too. The café by the gate is open at weekends and when something is happening on the place. The tipi stays up until October. The citrus trees, which have stood outside in pots all summer, are carried into the orangery before the first frosty night comes. The sauna feels better with every evening that cools.

We call the month’s full moon the Harvest Moon. It is full in the night between Wednesday 15 and Thursday 16 September, at 01.03. The name is our own, but it has a cousin in the English tradition, where the full moon nearest the autumn equinox is called the harvest moon. At this time of year the full moon rises at almost the same time several evenings in a row, and the moonlight comes straight after the sun has set – as though the day were lengthened for those not yet finished in the field.
himmel: The Harvest Moon is full in the night between 15 and 16 September. Between 14 and 18 September the moon rises each evening between about 18.35 and 18.45, in the east to east-north-east and before the sun has set. It is the small difference between the evenings – only a few minutes – that makes this full moon special. Around the spring full moon the moon can rise more than an hour and a half later each evening. In September it comes almost on the minute.

On Thursday 23 September at 08.01 the sun stands directly over the equator. It rises almost due east and sets almost due west, and it is a good day to check the compass directions from one of the photo points. Even so, the day is a little longer than twelve hours, 12 h 16 min, since the atmosphere lifts the sun’s disc above the horizon and we count from the sun’s upper edge. Day and night become equal only around 26 September.
citat: The balance lasts a day. The larder must last a winter.
manader.ingress: September is the month of gathering in. Day and night meet in the middle, and everything that has grown over the summer must be dealt with – eaten, stored, shared or saved as seed.

dates: On the second Saturday in September the city’s museums, churches, libraries and streets fill with events from the afternoon until late in the evening. In the jubilee year Uppsala University turns 550 and SLU, the Swedish University of Agricultural Sciences, 50.

In China and much of East Asia the moon festival is celebrated at the full moon of the eighth lunar month, this year on the evening of 15 September. Families gather, look at the moon and share mooncakes.
Full moon at 01.03 in the night before Thursday. On Wednesday evening the moon rises around 18.37, a good half hour before the sun sets.
The UN’s day of peace, when the world is urged to observe a day of ceasefire and non-violence. A day close to Vreta’s outlook.
At 08.01 the sun crosses the celestial equator heading south. The sun rises at 06.33 almost due east and sets at 18.49 almost due west.
At 12.20, the same day as the equinox. The moon is half light and half dark – like the day.
Michaelmas was one of the great boundaries of the farming year. The harvest was to be in, and the old year of service drew to its end.
At 04.35. The darkest nights of the month, good for stars and, if the sun is active, for the northern lights low in the north.

The Hindu nine nights in honour of the goddess Durga begin around 30 September–1 October and continue into October. The festival is celebrated differently in different regions, often with fasting, song and dance.
water: Ekoln
The autumn turnover begins. Zander and pike often bite well in autumn. The osprey migrates, and Lake Mälaren’s water level is on average at its lowest in September and October.
The fens
The reeds turn yellow. Geese and swans gather, and the cranes’ skeins pass over the fens heading south.
The tarn
The young frogs look for winter quarters. Leave stone piles and leaf heaps undisturbed around the tarn.
The pond
We stretch a net over parts of the pond, or skim off leaves regularly, so that not too many nutrients end up on the bottom.
events: Harvest weekend in the open ground
We lift potatoes, carrots and beetroot together and carry them down to the root cellar. Lunch in the outdoor kitchen from what we have dug up. Bring gloves – children especially welcome.

With a mushroom adviser in the woods around Vreta. We walk slowly, learn to tell the good mushrooms from the poisonous and clean the baskets at the long table. No mushroom goes to the kitchen without being checked.
The Harvest Moon by the pond

We gather by the pond just before 18.37 and watch the moon rise in the east while the sun has not yet set. Anyone who celebrates the Mid-Autumn Festival is welcome to bring mooncakes and tell us about it.
Juicing day with the neighbours’ apples
The neighbours come with their apples, and we mill and press in the old wooden press by the outdoor kitchen. Each person goes home with juice, and the pressings go to the hens and the compost.
At sunrise at 06.33 we stand at the fire place in the meadow and mark where the sun rises. Porridge and coffee in the orangery when the equinox occurs at 08.01.

The year’s biggest celebration. The long table is laid in the meadow with bread from the wood oven, soup from the harvest and juice from the press, for neighbours, guests and everyone who has helped during the year. With a little luck the cranes pass over us.
A work day after the festival.

We go through the year’s growing notes in the orangery and enter the harvest in the site journal: what grew, what failed and what we will do differently next year. The seed packets are labelled and sorted.
