watch: The passage of the cranes
Long skeins high over Vreta in the middle and at the end of September. The trumpeting is heard long before the flock is seen.
Dew in the spiders’ webs
Misty mornings make every web visible. Go out before the sun and take pictures from the photo points.
Deadly webcap
Grows in the same mossy spruce woods as the yellowfoot and can be mistaken for it. Red-brown, with a small point in the middle of the cap and rust-brown gills.
The first frost
Often comes at the end of September, first in the hollows by the pond. The citrus must be indoors before then.
The rising of the Harvest Moon
On 14–18 September the moon rises just after half past six, in the east to east-north-east and before the sun has set.
Elk by the road
The rut makes the elk restless, even at dusk. Drive calmly on the road to and from Vreta.
Young grass snakes
Small grass snakes leaving the compost. They are harmless and should be left in peace.
Northern lights
Low in the north during the dark nights around the new moon on 30 September. Best far from the lanterns.

manader.sub: Leaf fall, darkness and the lights that are lit
natur: In early and mid-October the autumn colours are usually at their strongest. As the days grow shorter and the nights colder the trees break down the green chlorophyll and move the nutrients to trunk and roots before winter. Then the yellow pigments that have been in the leaves all summer show through. The red is new. It forms in the leaves when the days are sunny and the nights cold, so the colours are strongest in years when October is clear. The oak is last of all. Young oaks often keep their brown leaves all winter.

The mushrooms continue into the frost. The yellowfoot tolerates a few cold nights and often grows in great numbers in the mossy spruce woods. The fly agarics stand red with white spots under the birches and at the meadow’s edge – lovely to look at and poisonous to eat. The same rule holds all autumn: never eat a mushroom you are not completely sure of. With the rains the mosses turn green again, and the lichens on the stone wall and the old oak’s bark brighten.

The migration continues. Geese and whooper swans pass over Ekoln, and the swans’ calls carry far. The thrushes migrate at night, and on a still, dark October evening you can hear the thin calls of redwings high above the farm. Towards the end of the month the first waxwings and bullfinches usually appear. The jay works from morning to evening carrying acorns from the oak and hiding them in the ground. The tawny owl calls often now, as the year’s young seek territories of their own and the old birds defend theirs.

The animals make ready for winter. The grass snake has crept into the compost or the stone wall, and the frogs have made their way to the bottom of the pond. The hedgehog eats everything it finds and looks for a leaf pile to sleep in. That is why we leave leaf piles and brush piles in the corners of the forest garden, and we feel carefully before moving them. The roe deer have changed into their grey-brown winter coats. The squirrels gather. In the hives the bees sit close in a ball around the queen when it turns cold.
karaktar: October is the month of colours and farewells. At the start of the month the birches glow yellow around the meadow, the rowan stands red and the aspen turns yellow and orange. Then comes a windy night, and the next day the colours lie on the ground. The tipi, which has stood in the meadow since April, is taken down. What was the summer’s outdoor life moves in – to the orangery, where the citrus trees now stand in shelter and the first fire will soon be lit in the fireplace, and to the workshops, where the autumn courses have begun.

The darkness shows every day. On 1 October the sun rises at 06.51 and sets at 18.25. On Saturday 30 October it sets at 17.02. The following night the clocks go back an hour, and on Sunday 31 October the sun sets as early as 15.59. Nothing has really happened to the light, only to the clock, but it feels different. The mornings grow lighter for a while – on the Sunday the sun rises at 07.05 instead of just after eight.

The work on the place moves from harvest to shelter. The beds are covered, the leaves raked, the water drained from the pipes and the animals prepared for winter. The café is open at weekends and when something is happening – on Cinnamon Bun Day, the Mushroom Moon evening and Diwali. Accommodation welcomes autumn retreats and course groups, and the sauna is fired every week. The orangery becomes the place’s gathering room, with the long table laid and the lemon trees in flower in the low light.

We call the month’s full moon the Mushroom Moon. It is full on Friday 15 October at 15.46 and rises the same afternoon just before 17.00, while the sun has not yet set. It takes its name from the forest. In October the yellowfoot chanterelles grow in the moss, the fly agarics glow red under the birches and the ground smells of mushrooms and damp leaves. It is the last great mushroom month before the frost takes over.
himmel: The Mushroom Moon is full on Friday 15 October at 15.46. It rises in the east-north-east just before 17.00, and for a while sun and moon stand on opposite sides of the sky – one on its way down in the west-south-west, the other on its way up. During the night it runs high across the south. The October moon stands higher than the summer full moons, and it lights the meadow so that the leaves cast shadows.

The planet of autumn is Saturn. On 18 October it is at opposition in the constellation of Pisces, directly opposite the sun. It rises in the east as the sun sets, stands in the south just after midnight and sets in the west at dawn. It shines steady and yellow-white, and in a small telescope both the rings and the largest moon, Titan, can be seen. Jupiter is back in the morning sky. In the middle of the month it rises in the east before 04.00 and shines brightly in Leo until dawn.
citat: A leaf that falls is not lost. It has only changed jobs.
manader.ingress: October takes down what the summer built up – the tipi, the leaves, the last apples. In return the candles are lit, and the fire moves indoors.
stat: 11 h 34 min
of daylight on 1 October in Uppsala. On 31 October 8 h 55 min remain – and on the same day winter time begins.
dates: The Jewish New Year 5788 begins at sunset. The shofar is blown, and apple dipped in honey is eaten for a sweet new year.
A fairly young Swedish tradition that has quickly become a given. Cinnamon, butter and sugar – and in many kitchens cardamom in the dough.
The elk hunt begins in Uppsala County and lasts until the end of January. Wear visible clothes in the forest, ideally orange, and keep the dog on a lead.
The Church of Sweden’s thanksgiving service for the harvest. Many churches are decorated with bread, fruit and vegetables from the district.
The Day of Atonement, the holiest day in the Jewish calendar, with fasting and prayer. It begins at sunset the evening before.
Full moon at 15.46. The moon rises in the east-north-east just before 17.00, before the sun has set.
The Feast of Tabernacles begins the evening before and lasts seven days. Meals are eaten in a hut roofed with branches, sparse enough to see the stars. It too is a harvest festival.
Saturn stands opposite the sun in the constellation of Pisces and can be seen all night. In a small telescope the rings show.
Shooting stars from dust left behind by Halley’s Comet. The moon is almost half and interferes, but the odd fast meteor may be seen after midnight.
A flag day. The UN Charter came into force on 24 October 1945.
The festival of light is celebrated by Hindus, Sikhs and Jains, this year on the same day as the new moon, at 15.36. Clay lamps are lit in windows and along paths – light over darkness.
The clocks go back an hour at 03.00. The mornings grow lighter, and the sun sets as early as 15.59.
Pumpkin lanterns and children in costume. The Swedish All Saints’ weekend (allhelgonahelgen) comes the weekend after, on 5–6 November.
water: Ekoln
Goldeneyes and goosanders gather on the bay, and the whooper swans rest on their way south. The boats are taken out before the ice comes.
The fens
The black-headed gulls are long gone, and the fens fall silent. The last ducks remain on the open water.
The tarn
The leaves fall into the tarn. The frogs go down into the mud on the bottom for the winter.
The pond
The grass snake goes into hibernation, often in the compost or under stones. The last leaves are skimmed off, and the deepest part of the pond is left in peace.
events: Cinnamon buns from the wood oven
The café has extra opening on Cinnamon Bun Day. We bake in the wood-fired oven from early morning, and in the afternoon the children of the neighbourhood shape their own buns.

On Harvest Thanksgiving we lay the long table in the orangery with the year’s harvest. Each person brings something they have grown, picked or made and tells what they want to give thanks for. The season’s first fire is lit in the fireplace.
We watch the moon rise just before 17.00 as the sun sets. Mushroom soup at the fire place and a short walk in the moonlight down to the pond.
Clay lamps in the ceramics workshop
We shape small lamps of clay, let them dry and fire them in the kiln. Whoever celebrates Diwali gets lamps for their festival, and whoever does not gets light for the November dark.
We set up the telescope in the meadow once it is dark and look at the rings and at Titan. Warm clothes, a warm drink and a short tour of the autumn constellations.

On Friday evening we light a last fire in the tipi and give thanks for the season. On Saturday it is taken down among the yellow birches: the canvas is dried and folded, the poles carried in and its place in the meadow raked.

If those who celebrate wish, clay lamps are lit along the stone path and on the granite boulders by the pond. Those who carry the tradition lead the evening. The rest of us help, listen and light a lamp if asked.
Pumpkin lanterns and the extra hour
The children hollow out pumpkins from the open ground for lanterns, and we take a short lantern walk at dusk, which now comes as early as four o’clock. Pumpkin soup in the orangery afterwards.

Feel carefully before a leaf pile is moved or brushwood burned. The hedgehog is looking for a winter nest now.

The first white mornings by the pond. A sign that the outdoor water should be drained.

manader.hand: The leaves to the earth. The candles to the darkness.

natur: In November it becomes clear what is evergreen. Once the leaves have fallen the moss glows on the stone wall and on the granite boulders by the pond, and the lichens on the oak’s furrowed bark gain a new clarity in the damp. In no month are the mosses as green as now. The lingonberry sprigs at the woodland edge keep their glossy leaves, and the spruces become the darkest thing in the landscape. On the hazel’s branches next year’s catkins already hang, small, grey-green and hard. They have sat there since late summer and are waiting for February.

The first ice on the pond comes on a clear, still night. It is thin as glass, catches leaves and needles in its surface and often breaks up again the next day. Nobody should walk on that ice – not children, not adults, not dogs. The frogs have made their way down to the bottom of the pond for the winter, and the grass snake has been asleep since October in a hollow under stones and roots. Out on Ekoln goldeneyes and goosanders gather on the open water, and the white-tailed eagles are seldom far away. When the bays freeze the birds move out towards open water, and the eagles usually follow.

The bird table in the apple tree is filled again when the cold comes. Great tits and blue tits find it the first day, the nuthatch and the marsh tit soon after. Some years the waxwings come as early as November and strip the rowans, and the bullfinches come down from the forest in pairs or small flocks. The suet hangs in metal holders and never in plastic nets, where birds can catch their claws.

The roe bucks shed their antlers from November, and whoever walks along the hedge may sometimes find one. The wild boar are in rut from November and for a couple of months on. The boars roam far, and their traces show as turned-up turf at the meadow’s edge and below the lilac hedge. The hedgehog has crept into a leaf pile and is asleep. So we do not turn the compost or move the leaf piles until spring.
karaktar: Once the leaves have fallen the skeleton of the place shows. The stone wall, which disappeared behind tall grass in summer, now lies bare and grey along the meadow. The old oak stretches its branches towards a low sky, and the outlines of the ponds can be seen all the way from the cottage steps. It smells of wet leaves, clay and firewood. The clay has soaked up the autumn rain, and in the hollows, where the groundwater stands high, the water glints between the tussocks. The tipi was packed away at the end of October. The meadow is mown, the raised beds are covered and the forest garden has gone to rest.

November is the month when Vreta turns inward. The work moves from the open ground to the workshops, the kitchen and the orangery. The winter courses begin in the joinery, the ceramics workshop, the sewing room and the smithy. The orangery becomes the living room of the place: the fire burns in the open fireplace in the limestone wall, the long table is laid for more than we are, and the lemon trees stand with both fruit and flowers in the glow of the candles. The café by the gate is open at weekends over All Saints and Father’s Day, then closes for a couple of weeks and opens again for Advent.

The light vanishes quickly. On 1 November the sun rises at 07.07 and sets at 15.57. On 30 November it rises at 08.17 and sets at 14.58, before three. Since the clocks changed to winter time at the end of October the dark comes in the middle of the afternoon, and it takes a few weeks to get used to. At midday at the end of the month the sun stands only eight or nine degrees above the horizon – about a hand’s breadth at arm’s length. The light becomes low and slanting. It lies in long streaks across the meadow and reaches under the orangery’s eaves all the way to the long table. Many days it never gets properly light at all, and the damp from Ekoln stands as mist over the meadow until midday.

We call the month’s full moon the Dark Moon. It is full on Sunday 14 November at 04.25, on the morning of Father’s Day. The name is our own, like all of Vreta’s moons, and it is not meant as a warning. November is the month when darkness takes up most room in everyday life – and the month when a full moon over frosty ground makes the greatest difference. On a clear night around the 14th the stone wall casts a sharp shadow across the meadow, and the paths can be seen without a torch.
himmel: The Dark Moon is full on Sunday 14 November at 04.25. Whoever goes out early on Father’s Day sees it standing a little way up in the west, above the meadow, while Jupiter shines clear in the south-east. The moon sinks towards the north-west as dawn comes. The same afternoon it rises again in the north-east, just after half past two and barely an hour before the sun sets. November’s full moon runs high through the night, and over frost or fresh snow it casts sharp shadows.

Saturn is the evening planet of autumn. It was at opposition in October and now shows in the south-east as it grows dark, highest in the south around half past nine. It shines with a steady, yellow-white light in the constellation of Pisces, where no bright stars compete. The rings, which stood edge-on a couple of years ago, have begun to open again. Jupiter rises in the east around one in the morning and stands high in the south as it grows light. Venus and Mars are too close to the sun to be seen.
citat: The darkness takes nothing from the place. It only shows what is already shining.
manader.ingress: November takes more than two hours of daylight. It is the month when we light the candles ourselves – for those who have gone before us and for what still waits.

manader.hand: Light the candle early and let the dark be dark.

natur: In December nature is as still as it can be. The trees are in deep dormancy, and the ground freezes from the top unless the snow gets there first. A thick snow cover insulates so well that the ground beneath it can stay near zero even when the air is twenty degrees colder. There, between the snow and the soil, voles and shrews live their winter lives in tunnels nobody sees until the thaw. They do best in winters when the snow comes early and stays.

The bird table in the apple tree is December’s stage. Great tits and blue tits come first and most often. The marsh tit takes a seed and flies off to hide it, the nuthatch walks head first down the trunk and the bullfinches sit still and chew. The yellowhammers, yellow as lemons against the snow, prefer to eat on the ground under the table. We feed sunflower seeds, oats and suet in metal holders, keep the table clean and dry and never let the food lie and go mouldy. Dirty bird tables spread disease between the birds.

In the spruces at the woodland edge a thin, high piping is heard. It is the goldcrest, one of Europe’s two smallest birds. It weighs about five grams and still survives cold nights, often by several huddling close together on a branch. The mountain hare has changed into its white winter coat. If the snow is late it shows from far off against the brown ground. The brown hare, its relative from the plains, stays brown all winter. The squirrel does not sleep through the winter but lives on the stores it buried in autumn. Many of the caches it never finds, and some of them become new hazel bushes and oaks.

Once the leaves have fallen the mistletoe shows in the limes, maples and apple trees of the Mälaren valley: dense green balls high in the crowns. It is evergreen and lives as a semi-parasite on the tree. The Uppsala area lies within its main Swedish range, and whoever has seen one mistletoe soon begins to see more along the roads. Mistletoe is protected. It may not be picked or damaged, so we look at it where it grows.
karaktar: December is the darkest month of the year, and at Vreta one of the liveliest. Outside everything rests. The pond has settled under ice, the raised beds sleep under leaves and spruce branches, and the hens go to roost as early as three o’clock. Indoors it is the opposite. The café and the shop by the gate open for the Advent weekends, St Lucia’s Day and the Christmas market. In the workshops the last of what is to be sold and given away is made. In the kitchen saffron buns and gingersnaps are baked, and in the orangery the Christmas table is laid among the lemon trees.

The orangery is the heart of December. Outside the old windows it is dark from early afternoon, but inside the fireplace burns in the limestone wall, the lemons turn yellow on the branches and the fig tree stands bare and waits. The minimum thermometer is read every morning. The citrus manages with a few degrees above zero, but frost damages both leaves and fruit, and whoever tends the fire last at night puts on an extra log when the sky is starry.

The weather cannot be relied on. Some years the snow lies white from the first Sunday of Advent, other years it is above zero and raining right up to New Year, and in recent years the grey version has been common. We plan for both. The Lucia procession walks in snow or in mud, and the solstice vigil is held by the fire whatever falls from the sky.

The sun rises at 08.19 on 1 December and sets at 14.56. In the middle of the month the day is 6 h 05 min, and around the solstice only a little over six hours. At midday on 22 December the sun stands barely seven degrees above the horizon. A curious feature is that the earliest sunset comes as early as the middle of the month, around 14.47, while the latest sunrise does not come until the days between Christmas and New Year. So the afternoons begin to lighten before the mornings do. The Winter Moon is full on St Lucia’s Day, Monday 13 December, at 17.08 – a coincidence we make the most of. The midwinter full moon runs highest of all full moons, just as the midsummer sun runs highest of all suns.
himmel: The Winter Moon is full on St Lucia’s Day at 17.08. It rises in the north-east early in the afternoon, before the sun has set, and when the Lucia procession sets off around five it stands low in the east-north-east over the birches. All night it climbs. At midnight it stands in the south, more than halfway up towards the zenith and higher than any other full moon of the year.

A day later, on the night between 14 and 15 December, the Geminids reach their maximum. They are usually the richest meteor shower of the year, with bright, slow shooting stars, and they come from the asteroid Phaethon. This year only the brightest show through the moonlight. It gets better at Christmas: the moon is new on Monday 27 December at 21.12, and the nights between Christmas and New Year are the darkest of the whole year. Orion stands in the south-east in the evening, and around nine Sirius rises beneath him, the brightest star in the sky. Sirius never climbs high at our latitudes and so twinkles red, blue and white through the cold air.
citat: We do not keep vigil to make the sun turn. We keep vigil to be there when it does.
manader.ingress: In December the darkness reaches its lowest point. In the night before the 22nd the sun turns – and almost everything we do this month is about keeping the light alive until then.

manader.sub: The year closes and begins again
natur: The first thing we compare is the soil, since it changes most slowly and tells the most. In the raised beds that have had leaves, compost and cover through four seasons the soil is darker and looser than a year ago, and last autumn’s spadefuls were full of worm tunnels. The clay in the hollows is unchanged. Clay changes over many years, not in one – and that too is worth writing down.

The pond has had a whole year. Under the ice the frogs sleep in the same mud as last winter. In the journal are the dates of what happened in between: when the ice let go, when the spawn was laid, when the dragonflies emerged, when the grass snake lay on its stone and when the ice settled again in November. We have also learned where the ice is usually weak – where the groundwater wells up at the edge and around the big granite boulders that are warmed by the sun. It is in the journal, with a small map.

The bird list is longer than a year ago. That is not only down to the birds. It is because we have learned to listen: the goldcrest’s thin piping in the spruces, the nuthatch’s whistle in the oak, the bullfinches’ soft contact call in the thickets. At the bird table it is the same guests as last year – great tits, blue tits, marsh tits and nuthatches. One clear morning at the end of the month the great tit begins to sing its spring song again. Last year we wrote down the date. This year we can compare.

The snow is still the best diary. On a morning after snowfall the fox’s track runs along the pond’s frozen edge in a calm arc between the granite boulders. Where the track suddenly ends in a pit of scattered snow, the fox has heard a vole under the snow and pounced. The stoat’s tracks go in pairs, in long bounds, and disappear into a pile of stones. The mountain hare’s large hind feet have passed under the lilac hedge, and the roe deer have browsed buds along the woodland edge. All of it remains for a few hours, until the wind or the next snowfall wipes it away.
karaktar: On 1 January 2028 the sun rises at 08.47 and sets at 14.58 – to the minute the same times as a year ago. Ice lies over the pond, snow or hoar frost over the meadow, and the old oak stands where it has always stood. Whoever looks only at the sky might think nothing has happened. The earth has gone once round the sun and is back in almost the same place in its orbit.

But the place is not the same. Under the snow lies a year of leaves that have become humus, a year of roots that have gone deeper and a mowing that has taken the meadow a first step towards becoming leaner and richer in flowers. In the site journal there are twelve months of notes: when the ice went and when it settled, when the frogspawn lay at the sun-warmed edge, when the swifts came and when the cranes headed south. January 2028 is the month when we read all of it – and see what it says.

So this is not a month for starting again from the beginning. It is a month for closing a year properly before the next is opened. Christmas is carried out on St Knut’s Day, the tools are sharpened and what was worn during the year is mended. On the oak table lies the site journal’s year book with pressed flowers between the pages and the photo points’ pictures in rows – the same view, month after month, a whole year.

The Ice Moon returns on Wednesday 12 January, ten days earlier than last year, and it comes with a small lunar eclipse in the morning dark. Twelve lunar cycles are almost eleven days shorter than a solar year. That is why the full moons wander backwards through the calendar, year by year, until there is room for a thirteenth. We have followed them all: the Ice Moon, the Light Moon, the Sap Moon, the Frog Moon, the Nettle Moon, the Bright Moon, the Haymaking Moon, the Berry Moon, the Harvest Moon, the Mushroom Moon, the Dark Moon, the Winter Moon – and now the Ice Moon again.
himmel: The Ice Moon is full on Wednesday 12 January at 05.02. By around 04.45 it has already begun to slide into the earth’s umbra. It is a small partial eclipse. The umbra reaches only a narrow piece of the moon’s edge – greatest around 05.13 – and the partial phase lasts about an hour, from around 04.45 to around 05.45. From about four o’clock the penumbra can be sensed as a grey veil over one side of the moon’s disc. The moon then stands a good way up in the west, and it is completely dark; dawn begins only after 06.00. At the same time Jupiter shines clear in the south. A lunar eclipse is safe to watch, with the naked eye or through binoculars.

When the book began Venus stood as the morning star in the south-east. A year later it has changed sides. fyravatten_p: Ekoln is the northernmost bay of Lake Mälaren, 22 square kilometres in size, with a broad middle and four arms. The Fyris river flows into the north-eastern arm. In the south-west the bay ends at Varpsund and at Lårstaviken, where the Örsundaån flows in. In the south-east the water continues through Skofjärden and Erikssund towards Sigtunafjärden, and on towards Stockholm and the sea. Ekoln is known for its zander fishing, and it often freezes late. In many winters the whole bay freezes only some way into January. When the ice bears it becomes one of Uppland’s great skating rinks.

Right next to Vreta udde lies the Hammarskog nature area with two bird-rich fens, Dalkarlskärret and Stora kärret, and the reed beds of Dalbyviken. From the bird towers you can see grebes, coots, swans and harriers, and in spring the bittern booms in the reeds. The fens are shallow and freeze early. Dalkarlskärret usually gets the municipality’s first ploughed natural ice.

At Vreta Solglänta there are two waters of our own. The tarn is the small pond, about 25 square metres. It is shallow, warms first in spring and freezes first in autumn, and it is fish-free, so it becomes the amphibians’ nursery. The pond is about 125 square metres, natural and edged with grey and pink granite boulders, with a small islet and a young birch. There the grass snake suns itself on its stone, the newts swim and the dragonflies patrol. There are the sauna, the steps of stone and oak and, in winter, the ice hole.
forord: There is a day every winter when you suddenly notice that it is still light at four o’clock. It has been going on for weeks, a few minutes at a time, but on that particular day it shows. Someone stands at the window in the cottage and says it aloud: it is lighter now. And so the year begins again – not on New Year’s night, but in that moment.

This book is about such moments. About the day the great tit begins to sing, the evening the frogs spawn in the pond, the night it no longer grows dark and the morning the first frost lies on the meadow. About full moons and new moons, solstices and equinoxes, Candlemas and Walpurgis Night, Midsummer and All Saints. And about all the work that lets a place like Vreta Solglänta live through a whole year: the sowing and the harvest, the tools sharpened, the bees put to bed for winter, the rooms made up and the fire lit.

The book follows thirteen months, from January 2027 up to and including January 2028. That is deliberate. A year is not quite finished until you have come back to where you began and can see the difference: that the soil has darkened where the compost has lain, that there are more frogs in the pond, that the bird list has grown longer and that an apple tree planted last year bears its first fruit. The thirteenth month is the one that makes the circle visible.
klockor: The clock most of us live by is the calendar on the wall: twelve months, fifty-two weeks, holidays in red. It is practical and necessary. But on a place like Vreta it soon becomes clear that it is not enough. There are other clocks running at the same time, and they decide more of what happens than the calendar does.

The first is the sun. It decides how much light there is, and the light decides almost everything else. At the winter solstice the day in Uppsala is only six hours long. At the summer solstice it is almost nineteen, and the night never grows dark. Between them lie the equinoxes, when day and night are roughly the same length. It is the sun’s year that decides when seeds can be sown, when the birds come and when the hens begin to lay again.

The second is the moon. It goes round in roughly twenty-nine and a half days, which gives twelve or thirteen full moons in a year. The moon affects the tides of the oceans but hardly the growing in a garden in Uppland. Even so, we follow it. It gives the year a breath roughly once a week – new moon, waxing, full moon, waning – and several of the place’s gatherings have their place in that rhythm.

The third is nature itself: the warmth in the soil, the water in the pond and the living creatures’ own clocks. It does not go by date but by temperature, day length and weather. The frogs spawn when the ice has gone and the water has grown warm enough, not on a particular day in April. The bird cherry flowers when it has had enough warmth. That clock runs fast some years and slow in others.

The fourth is people’s: the festivals, the traditions, school holidays and summer holidays – and the place’s own rhythm, with a seasonal café, retreats, courses and work days. That clock we have set ourselves. But it is older than it looks. Many of the Swedish festivals lie close to the sun’s turning points: Christmas at the winter solstice, Midsummer at the summer solstice, Easter at the first full moon after the spring equinox.
